bluf: Common Thread Collective is a US ecommerce profit partner for mid market DTC brands that sells forecasting, measurement, media buying and creative as one operating system, the Prophit Engine, launched in 2026. The Horus read places it Favored at 22.4, best placed for KJ9, with 3 of 3 house tests practised. Where it is going is software plus one operator, pitched as one Prophit Engineer replacing four specialists. A rival should know that the record names only 2 clients, both logos, and that the headline numbers (33% revenue, 42% contribution margin, within 3% of forecast) are claims with no case study behind them.
doing:
Common Thread Collective positions as an ecommerce profit partner for DTC brands, running forecasting, measurement, media buying and creative through its Prophit Engine operating system: it buys Meta and Google ads for consumer brands and sells the forecast and margin model around the buying as the product. Its headline claim is that across clients the Prophit Engine delivered 33% YoY revenue and 42% contribution margin growth, landing within 3% of forecast; no case study text sits behind the claim.

The sold mix leads with data and measurement, scored 3, on the homepage headline that the Prophit Engine runs forecasting, modeling, incrementality and measurement as one system. Paid search and paid social score 2 and are core: a Google Ad Buying service and methodology page with a case result of 191% more purchase conversions via Google Demand Gen, and Meta Ad Buying as the first listed service with a Meta methodology page and Snapchat and AppLovin case results. The service list adds TikTok Shop and Ad Creative; proprietary lines are the Prophit Engine, the Prophit System and The DTC Index. SEO, creator, email and CRM, web and B2B score 0, and the record lists no partner badges.

Its AI posture treats AI as new paid surfaces: it tracks ChatGPT Ads and Google AI Mode shopping weekly, and the Prophit Engine pitch is software plus one operator. The one dated move is the 2026 launch of the Prophit Engine, software plus a dedicated Prophit Engineer, which the homepage in Sep 2026 calls just launched. Pricing signal: enterprise sophistication at a fraction of the cost, one Prophit Engineer replacing four specialists, no prices shown. It runs its own media arm: the Ecommerce Playbook podcast, DTC Hotline, The Thread newsletter and The DTC Index. Conspicuously absent: an office list, ownership, founding year, headcount, any case study or job in the deep record, and any sitemap update in 365 days.
clients:
The record reads the client type as mid market and the verticals as DTC ecommerce and consumer brands; the home market is the US, with no office list. The needs read holds 2 clients, both client logos on the case studies page and both named only: Maui Jim and The Honest Kitchen, with nothing about the work, so their needs are inferred from the sold mix as paid performance and data and measurement. No client is shared with another tracked agency. The capability notes carry results without names: 191% more purchase conversions via Google Demand Gen, and Snapchat and AppLovin results, so the record shows work it cannot attach to a client. For a commerce agency whose headline claim aggregates across clients and whose LinkedIn ad cites $3B in GMV, a book of 2 logos is the finding: the proof is presented as a portfolio number, not as named accounts.

What the base needs next: KJ9 (measurement gets worse before it gets better) is the judgment the Horus read places it best for, and KJ5 (the price of attention splits in two) the one it is most exposed to through paid social and programmatic. It is very likely, moderate confidence, that DTC brands buying Meta and Google media will keep paying for incrementality and forecasting as attribution degrades, which is the line it leads with; it is likely, low confidence, that the same brands will push the buying hours into platform automation, which is what KJ4 describes and what a one operator pitch already concedes.
house: Say and do: three lines tested, three practised, integrity 100. Paid search is corroborated: it runs its own Google ads, 131 in the Transparency Center and 6 in the last 30 days, 128 of them video and 3 text, last shown 2026-09-25. Paid social is corroborated by Meta and LinkedIn Insight pixels, and LinkedIn advertising by 2 company page ads, one reading 'We replaced 4 specialists with 1 Prophit Engineer. 42% CM growth. Within 3% of forecast. Across $3B in GMV' and the other promoting an Ecommerce CFO Summit built around forecasting. The Radar flagged no gaps. The house runs on Shopify with GTM, HubSpot and Hotjar alongside the pixels; no test tools or ABM stack. It publishes an llms.txt and blocks no AI crawlers; the sitemap lists 897 URLs, 13 of them AI URLs, with 0 updated in 90 days and 0 in 365 days. Meta and TikTok library readings are absent from the record.
market:
Horus puts Common Thread Collective at tailwind index 22.4, band Favored, 17:15 on the Solar Arc. Best placed for KJ9 (measurement gets worse before it gets better, driven by Data & Measurement) and KJ1 (the click replaced by the citation). Most exposed to KJ5 (the price of attention splits in two, driven by Paid Social and Programmatic & CTV) and KJ4 (the platforms absorbing the execution layer). Best scenario fit: The Walled Oasis at 60/100. It is making P4 and P8 (ads inside assistants with holdout or incrementality measurement to test them), partial on P1, absent on P2, P6 and P7; P3 does not apply, P5 unknown.

The Monsoon read is 45.3, band Breeze, percentile 17: migration 42.8 against displacement 47.8. The sold mix supplies 43 of the index, Data & Measurement (14) and Paid Search (12) carrying the most movable hours; the work would go 65% to South and Southeast Asia and 25% to Latin America, and automation overlaps 45%. The footprint is inferred: no hub offices, no onshore claims, mid market client type adding 5 points.
openings:
The book is the opening: 2 clients on record, both logos, for an agency whose headline claim aggregates 33% revenue and 42% contribution margin growth across clients and whose LinkedIn ad cites $3B in GMV. A rival pitching DTC brands can very likely (moderate confidence) ask for the named accounts behind the portfolio number, which the public record cannot supply. Falsifier: a later compile adding named case studies with described work closes this opening.

Lead with the one operator pitch: enterprise sophistication at a fraction of the cost, four specialists replaced by one Prophit Engineer, and no prices shown (P5 unknown), so a transparent outcome priced offer is a conversation it cannot have in public. Displacement at 47.8 says the book does not buy on price, so the undercut is on proof of incrementality rather than rate. It sells no SEO, content, CRM or creator work (all scored 0): a rival pairing the same measurement story with owned audience and organic lines (P7 absent here) offers what the Prophit Engine does not. Its sitemap shows 0 updates in 90 days against a media arm of podcast, hotline, newsletter and index: the publishing story and the crawlable house disagree.
